rules.title: Confirm the need before building
rules.what: Do not write code for a feature whose user need is unverified. Confirm the need with evidence (user research, existing usage data, a real requester), and prefer reuse or a non-digital route where suitable.
rules.why: The greenest feature is the one that is never built. A well-optimised solution to a need nobody has still costs every resource it took to build and run.
rules.how: Before building: who needs it, for what task, what do they do today instead? If the answer is a guess, say so and get evidence before investing more than a prototype.

verify.how: A dated statement of the user task and the evidence backing it exists for any new feature.

limits: Code cannot establish adoption; a need hypothesis is not a verified need.

rules.title: Apply the 3U before investing
rules.what: For a new service, feature or AI pilot, assess the 3U: utile (does it help?), utilisé (is it actually used when needed?), utilisable (can people complete the task?).
rules.why: The 3U separate value from waste better than any technical metric: a fast, efficient service nobody uses is pure waste, whatever its EcoIndex.
rules.how: One essential task, its current alternative, a few observed users, a short observation period. Record numerators and denominators; before launch, usage is unverified, not failed.

verify.how: A 3U worksheet exists with task, sample, period, results and gaps disclosed.

limits: Small samples are starting points, not proof of population-wide fit.

rules.title: Keep features to what is needed
rules.what: Every feature must trace to a need. Cut or refuse features that serve no stated user task, including features built 'because we can'.
rules.why: Feature count drives every downstream resource: code to write, surface to load, paths to test, maintenance forever. Fewer features is the cheapest optimisation.
rules.how: When a request arrives, name the user task it serves. No task, no feature. Offer the lighter alternative that serves the task.

verify.how: The feature list maps to user tasks; orphans are flagged.

limits: Removing an authorised feature needs the owner's decision, not the reviewer's.

rules.title: Support older devices and slow networks
rules.what: Define the minimum supported device, browser and connectivity profiles from the intended audience, and keep the essential journey working there.
rules.why: Extending the useful life of existing devices is one of the strongest levers of digital sobriety: the hardware footprint dominates the usage footprint for most services.
rules.how: State minimum profiles, test the essential journey on them, and check that new requirements do not exclude devices that were fine yesterday. Never retain a vulnerable dependency solely to keep compatibility.

patterns.note: Very short browserslist defaults may exclude older devices; check against the declared audience.

verify.how: Essential journey tested on the declared minimum profile (device/browser/network).

limits: Security support overrides device longevity: never keep a vulnerable path for old hardware.

rules.title: User control over engagement mechanics
rules.what: No autoplaying media, no engagement-only infinite scroll, no unsolicited refresh, prefetch or notifications. Let users finish a task and stop.
rules.why: Mechanics that hold attention consume resources without adding value, and they take control away from the user. Both are waste by definition.
rules.how: Require an explicit action to start media; bound or paginate lists; make notifications opt-in; verify idle behaviour (no network or CPU when the user is not acting).

patterns.note: Autoplay attribute; verify no user-gesture gate around it.

verify.how: Idle-state network/CPU check shows no background activity; media start requires user action.

limits: Bounded pagination must remain keyboard-navigable and assistive-tech friendly.

rules.title: Environmental criteria in user stories
rules.what: Express sobriety requirements as acceptance criteria in the user story, so they are testable like any other requirement.
rules.why: A sobriety wish that lives outside the acceptance criteria is not implemented, it is hoped for. Inside, it gets estimated, tested and reviewed.
rules.how: Add measurable criteria to the story: page weight budget, max queries per view, payload cap, device profile to support.

verify.how: Stories for touched features carry at least one measurable sobriety criterion.

rules.title: Plan retirement from the start
rules.what: For features, content and environments, define an owner and a review date; plan how they will be retired (export, retention, restore, dependency checks).
rules.why: Services accrete features nobody uses, running on environments nobody shuts down. Without a retirement plan, everything built runs forever.
rules.how: When creating a feature or environment, record owner and review date. Recommend cleanup from evidence of disuse; get authority before deleting production data or disabling a service.

verify.how: Inventory of features/environments with owner and last-review date exists.

limits: Retiring a live service is a business decision; the rule ensures it is a conscious one.

rules.title: Assess third-party services before integrating
rules.what: Before adding a third-party service or script, assess its value, weight, data practices and failure mode; load it only where and when it contributes.
rules.why: Third-party scripts are invisible weight: they run on every page load, add requests, and shift costs to the user's device without ever appearing in your bundle size.
rules.how: List what the script does for the user task, its measured weight, and what breaks without it. Load on demand, after consent where required, with a fallback.

patterns.note: Third-party script tag; verify it serves the page's task and is loaded deliberately.

verify.how: Each external script has a stated purpose, measured weight and loading condition.

limits: Some third parties (payment, consent, analytics under consent) are legitimate; the rule forces deliberation, not abstinence.
